title: Co-aging reference cell that leaks in lockstep with data
idea: Worse: compare every leaking cell against a fixed VDD/2 reference so margin shrinks every millisecond. Flip: each row carries a few reference cells written to a half level at the same instant as the data, through identical access transistors, so the reference droops with the data and the sense amp compares against a co-aged threshold.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): most '1' margin loss is common-mode droop; tracking it could stretch retention 2-4x and cut refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~50-75%.

title: Near-miss flagging sense amps drive traffic-based adaptive refresh
idea: Worse: refresh every row at worst-case 64 ms because nobody knows which cells are weak. Flip: add a cheap offset-biased secondary latch per sense-amp group that flags reads whose signal landed near the trip point during normal traffic; flagged rows enter a small refresh-priority table while all other rows run 4-8x longer refresh intervals.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): retention-aware refresh with no offline profiling; ~50-70% refresh reduction at 32-64 Gb.

title: Two-transistor analog charge integrators count activations per wordline
idea: Worse: let rows be hammered with zero memory of past activations. Flip: every local wordline driver deposits a fixed charge packet on a per-row leaky MOS integrator at each activation; a shared comparator in the driver strip samples it on activation and fires neighbor refresh when it crosses threshold, while the leak resets it naturally each window.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): per-row tracking for every row in ~2-3 transistors instead of SRAM counter tables.

title: Time-domain sense amps race delay lines at 0.6 V arrays
idea: Worse: insist on full 1 V voltage swings and amplitude margin on every bitline. Flip: let the bitline differential set the bias of two current-starved delay stages and resolve which edge arrives first with a time comparator, so a ~0.6 V array supply still yields a clean decision.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): bitline CV^2 energy drops ~60% if VARY goes from 1.0 to 0.6 V, with less access-transistor stress.

title: Ferroelectric negative-capacitance liner shrinks effective bitline capacitance
idea: Worse: make bitline capacitance as large as possible so the transfer ratio collapses. Flip: place a thin, stabilized ferroelectric layer in series within the bitline-to-neighbor spacer dielectric so its negative capacitance cancels part of the parasitic, lowering effective C_BL and amplifying the charge-sharing signal.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): signal ~ Cs/(Cs+CBL); halving effective CBL nearly doubles signal, allowing lower-AR capacitors or 2x longer bitlines with half the sense amps.

title: Resonant LC tank charges wordlines adiabatically and recycles energy
idea: Worse: slam 3 V wordlines up from ground and dump their charge to ground on every activation. Flip: drive the selected wordline group from a package-level inductor in a resonant loop that ramps it up sinusoidally and swings the charge back into the tank, or into the next wordline, on deactivation.
why: Voltage floor and activation energy (fact 10): recovers ~50-70% of wordline CV^2 energy and offloads the VPP pumps.

title: Backside-built sense amplifiers connect through bitline-pitch nano-vias
idea: Worse: lay periphery beside the array where it eats half the die. Flip: after the front-side array, bond to a carrier, thin to under a micron as in backside power delivery, and layer-transfer low-temperature transistors for sense amps and sub-wordline drivers onto the backside, contacting bitlines through nano-vias at bitline pitch.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): folding periphery under the array shrinks die ~35-40% and raises bits per wafer without litho scaling.

title: Module PMIC supplies wordline high voltage, deleting on-die charge pumps
idea: Worse: generate the 3 V wordline rail and negative back-bias on every die with ~30%-efficient charge pumps. Flip: supply VPP and VBB from GaN or switched-capacitor converters on the module PMIC through dedicated bumps and package planes, deleting on-die pumps and their reservoir capacitors.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and voltage-floor energy (fact 10): frees ~4-6% of die and lifts VPP efficiency from ~30% to ~85%.

title: Ship lightly repaired dies with exported bad-row maps, NAND-style
idea: Worse: scrap any die whose defects exceed on-die fuse and spare-row capacity, and keep growing redundancy area. Flip: ship dies with minimal spares plus an exported defect and weak-row map that the memory controller uses to remap rows, the way NAND controllers handle bad blocks.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and supply: shrinks fuse/spare area 2-3% and recovers 5-15% of discarded dies, directly raising usable bit supply.

title: Isolated early-latch sensing with parity-checked deferred restore
idea: Worse: wait for every bitline to fully develop under worst-case corners before latching. Flip: latch at half the usual development time with isolation gates cutting the latch off from the bitlines, ship data out, and write back only after a per-burst parity check passes; on a rare mismatch the still-intact shared bitline charge is re-latched with more time.
why: Latency, bandwidth and read energy: ~30% lower tRCD at typical corners while keeping worst-case correctness.

title: Tungsten-free wordlines driven from both ends with mid-line repeaters
idea: Worse: keep buried wordlines dependent on tungsten, ~80% sourced from China. Flip: switch to supply-safe TiN or doped-poly fill and offset its higher resistance by splitting each local wordline into halves driven from both ends plus a mid-array boost repeater in the sub-wordline driver strip.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (tungsten chokepoint) while holding wordline RC within ~10% of today.

title: Hybrid-bonded area pads above each bank replace the global datapath
idea: Worse: haul every bit across the die through global I/O lines and serializers to edge pads. Flip: place hybrid-bonded area-array pads directly above each bank's column logic so a logic die below reads each bank locally, deleting global I/O buses and most serializers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and periphery area (fact 7): <1 pJ/bit access and ~8-10% of die freed.

title: Segmented sub-wordline gates activate only the requested 512-byte slice
idea: Worse: open an entire 8 KB row to read 64 bytes. Flip: insert segment-select transistors in the sub-wordline drivers so only the cells and sense amps of one 512 B slice connect and fire, leaving the rest of the row untouched.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): activation energy per useful bit drops ~10-16x and row-hammer exposure per activation shrinks.

title: Charge-redistribution SAR sensing stores three levels per cell
idea: Worse: spend all margin storing a single bit per cell. Flip: share the bitline charge onto binary-weighted reference capacitors in a two-step successive-approximation sense amp that resolves three charge levels (1.58 bits/cell), Gray-coded so a one-level slip becomes a single-bit ECC-correctable error.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~58% more bits per cell area if the signal margin holds.

title: Back-gate trimmed tiny sense amps replace large matched pairs
idea: Worse: make sense-amp transistors huge so random mismatch stays below the signal. Flip: shrink sense-amp devices 3-4x and cancel each pair's offset with a per-column back-gate voltage programmed at wafer test from a shared trim DAC row and held as a fuse code.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-amp strips ~40-50% smaller while tolerating smaller cell signals.

title: One-hot token ring steps refresh without waking address decoders
idea: Worse: run the full row decoder and predecode buses for every refresh command. Flip: a one-hot shift chain embedded in the wordline driver strip passes a token row to row during refresh and streaming scans, so decoders and global address buses stay power-gated.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): periphery share of refresh energy cut ~25-35%.

title: Bank-to-bank charge recycling during bitline precharge
idea: Worse: dump each bank's charged bitlines back to the VDD/2 rail and pay again to charge another bank. Flip: before equalizing, connect the high-side bitlines of a closing bank through a charge-transfer switch to the bitlines of the bank about to restore, so charge is reused instead of wasted.
why: Energy per bit (facts 8, 10): ~30-40% of bitline swing energy recovered on interleaved workloads.

title: Segmented cell-plate kick boosts read signal before charge sharing
idea: Worse: hold the cell plate at a static VDD/2 so the signal is only what Cs alone delivers. Flip: split the plate into per-mat segments and pulse the selected mat's plate by a few hundred mV during the read to couple extra charge onto the bitline, then return it before restore.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): ~20-30% more signal from the same ~5 fF, buying aspect-ratio relief or longer bitlines.

title: Inductive coil links replace signal TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Worse: drill thousands of signal TSVs through every die and lose area and yield. Flip: put small spiral coils in top metal for near-field inductive data links between thinned stacked dies, keeping only a few large power TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): signal-TSV keep-out area and much TSV-related yield loss removed.

title: Per-segment adaptive negative wordline bias tames the leakage tail
idea: Worse: hold every unselected wordline at the same off level so the leakiest 0.01% of cells set refresh for all. Flip: give each wordline segment a test-programmed negative off level (-0.2 to -0.4 V) from a small local bias generator, applying deep negative bias only where the tail lives.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): ~10x tail suppression in hot spots stretches refresh 2-4x while sparing gate stress elsewhere.

title: Open-source DRAM periphery IP library on a U.S. foundry
idea: Worse: keep sense-amp, decoder and pump know-how locked inside three companies. Flip: a federally funded consortium publishes silicon-proven sense amps, wordline drivers, charge pumps and test macros on a U.S. mature node, so startups pairing novel cells with standard periphery need not reinvent it.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: removes years of periphery design time and cost for new entrants.

title: U.S. mature logic fabs build control dies; DRAM fabs only arrays
idea: Worse: build control periphery on scarce, EUV-laden DRAM wafer starts. Flip: contract control, I/O, pump and test dies to U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundries and hybrid-bond them to array-dense dies from DRAM fabs that keep only bitline sense amps and spend the rest of the wafer on bits.
why: Capital intensity and supply: ~30-40% more bits per DRAM-fab wafer start, using underused U.S. logic capacity.

title: All-zero row tags let periphery answer reads without activation
idea: Worse: sense and restore 8 KB of zeros exactly like useful data. Flip: keep a per-row pattern tag in a small SRAM in the bank periphery; rows tagged all-zero or repeated-pattern are answered by the column logic without activating the row and skipped by refresh until written.
why: Refresh and overfetch (facts 3, 8): zero or duplicate pages are often 10-30% of memory; their refresh and activation energy goes to ~0.

title: Micro-transfer-printed periphery dielets onto array-only wafers
idea: Worse: build every decoder, pump and I/O block in the same costly, EUV-heavy DRAM process. Flip: fabricate pre-tested periphery dielets on cheap logic wafers, release them, and elastomer-stamp transfer-print thousands per pass onto array-only DRAM wafers, then print or plate the short interconnects.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7) and capital: DRAM wafer area goes ~90% to cells and only known-good periphery is placed, raising bits per wafer ~1.6x.

title: Inkjet-printed conductive links perform redundancy repair at sort
idea: Worse: burn area on fuse banks, antifuse programming pumps and laser-fuse windows. Flip: at wafer sort an inkjet printer deposits silver or copper nanoparticle links on a top-level link field that sets the spare-address compare bits fuses normally hold, programmed straight from the test map.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): deletes ~1-3% of die in fuse area and fuse-read logic with maskless per-die repair.

title: Inkjet-printed personality layer turns one die into many SKUs
idea: Worse: tape out separate masks and dies for each width, density bin and speed grade. Flip: leave the final configuration via layer unpatterned and inkjet-print jumpers per wafer to set I/O width, bank grouping, redundancy and timing options, so one mask set serves the whole product line.
why: Capital intensity (masks) and supply agility: fabs shift output between products in days instead of quarters.

title: Roll-to-roll high-k decoupling film laminated onto the die
idea: Worse: fill periphery with MOS decoupling capacitors to keep supply noise down. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-coated thin-film decoupling sheet, such as a BaTiO3-polymer nanocomposite between foil electrodes, onto the die top or package through a printed bump array.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): on-die decap is several percent of die; moving it to a laminate frees area and adds lower-inductance bulk capacitance.

title: Aerosol-jet printed edge wiring connects staircase-stacked memory dies
idea: Worse: drill TSVs through every HBM die. Flip: stack dies in an offset staircase with printed insulating ramps and aerosol-jet-print signal and power traces down the exposed edges, connecting pads tier to tier with no through-silicon vias.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area or TSV yield loss; cheaper stacking for capacity tiers.

title: Printed thermistor film maps hotspots for per-bank refresh rates
idea: Worse: refresh every bank at the hottest corner's rate. Flip: laminate a printed thermistor array film (NTC oxide or carbon ink) over each die or under the lid, read by the controller to set each bank's refresh from its true local temperature.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention roughly halves every ~10 C, so cool banks can refresh 2-4x less, cutting refresh energy ~20-40%.

title: Print-on-die carbon-nanotube TFT layer hosts slow control logic
idea: Worse: spend DRAM silicon on mode registers, BIST engines, temperature sensors and power-up sequencers that run at kHz-MHz. Flip: after passivation, inkjet-print a low-temperature carbon-nanotube TFT circuit layer on top of the die to host those slow functions, wired down through pad openings.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~5-10% of die moved off silicon onto a cheap printed layer.

title: Roll-to-roll polymer waveguide flex carries memory traffic optically
idea: Worse: push every bit through lossy copper with power-hungry SerDes equalizers. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-embossed polymer waveguide flex between memory stacks and the processor package, coupled to micro-LED or VCSEL transmitters on the memory base die.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): sub-pJ/bit links over centimeters, letting memory sit farther from the accelerator and escape interposer area limits.

title: Printed nanoparticle varistor film takes over ESD protection duty
idea: Worse: guard every I/O pad with large on-die ESD clamps that add capacitance and area. Flip: screen-print a ZnO-nanoparticle varistor film between I/O traces and ground on the package substrate so surges clamp off-die, letting on-die clamps shrink to minimal size.
why: Periphery area and I/O energy: smaller clamps cut pad capacitance ~30-50% and free I/O ring area.

title: Printed passive equalizer networks replace on-die CTLE and FFE
idea: Worse: keep growing active equalizers and DFE taps inside every DRAM I/O. Flip: print resistor-capacitor-inductor equalization networks (gravure-printed thin-film R and C, printed spiral L) on the package or module flex at each lane to pre-shape the channel passively.
why: Periphery area and I/O power: removes ~10-20% of PHY power and area.

title: Roll-to-roll conductive-elastomer probe film for full-wafer parallel test
idea: Worse: test DRAM with costly MEMS probe cards a few dies at a time and pack extra test logic onto every die. Flip: use a disposable roll-to-roll-printed anisotropic conductive-elastomer film that contacts every pad on the wafer at once, fanned out through a printed flex to the tester.
why: Test cost and test-periphery area: full-wafer parallelism lowers test cost per bit and the on-die test-compression logic needed.

title: Roll-to-roll anodized alumina templates for ultra-high-aspect capacitors
idea: Worse: keep the cell signal tiny so sense amps must stay large and bitlines short. Flip: grow nanoporous anodic alumina continuously on a roll-to-roll aluminum line, transfer the AR>200 pore film onto the array, and ALD-coat the pores into capacitors, with storage-node pads wider than the pore pitch so each node captures several pores.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AR 115+ without deep etch; more signal lets sense amps shrink and bitlines lengthen.

title: Printed oxide-TFT glass interposer performs die and bank selection
idea: Worse: repeat chip-select, rank and bank-group muxing logic inside every DRAM die and buffer chip. Flip: build a glass-panel interposer with inkjet-printed oxide TFT switches that set, per page epoch, which of dozens of simple array dies drive each high-speed lane, consolidating selection periphery into one cheap printed layer.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: panel printing costs ~100x less per cm^2 than silicon, and array dies shed redundant control logic.

title: Jet-and-flash nanoimprint patterns all relaxed-pitch periphery layers
idea: Worse: expose even relaxed periphery metal layers on immersion or EUV scanners at full scanner capex. Flip: print periphery interconnect and contact layers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint templates, reserving scanners for array-critical layers.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): nanoimprint tools cost ~1/3-1/5 of a scanner per layer and use far less power.

title: Roll-to-roll laminated microchannel film cools hot periphery strips
idea: Worse: let pumps, PHYs and base-die logic heat the array so refresh doubles above 85 C. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-embossed polymer microchannel film with printed manifolds onto the stack, routing coolant directly over hot periphery strips and keeping array tiers below ~70 C.
why: Refresh (fact 3): staying out of the 2x-refresh temperature range halves refresh energy and bandwidth loss in HBM.

title: Roll-to-roll imprinted fan-out film replaces silicon interposer for HBM
idea: Worse: wire HBM to the GPU on large, expensive silicon interposers limited by reticle stitching. Flip: produce 2 um line/space redistribution films by roll-to-roll UV imprint and plating on polyimide, laminated as an organic interposer carrying the memory PHY lanes.
why: Capital intensity and HBM cost: interposer cost per mm^2 drops ~5-10x and size is no longer reticle-limited.

title: Printed trimmable reference ladder on package feeds bitline references
idea: Worse: replicate bandgaps, reference generators and trim fuses for VBLP, VREF and VPLATE on every die. Flip: print a ruthenium-oxide or carbon resistor ladder on the package substrate, laser- or inkjet-trimmed at final test, delivering filtered reference voltages to every die in the package.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): removes ~1-2% of die in analog reference circuitry and improves matching across a stack.

title: Fund U.S. roll-to-roll advanced-packaging lines for memory periphery layers
idea: Worse: leave printed and laminated packaging layers to offshore suppliers so every module ships through Asia. Flip: CHIPS-style grants and offtake guarantees for U.S. roll-to-roll lines making organic interposers, decap laminates and printed repair and configuration layers for domestic memory assembly.
why: U.S. manufacturability: printed lines cost ~$50-200M versus $15B fabs and onshore the periphery and packaging share of memory value.

title: Repurpose OLED inkjet lines to print panel-level memory interposers
idea: Worse: build all new memory packaging capacity from scratch. Flip: convert idle Gen-6/8 OLED inkjet-printing and TFT lines into panel-level printers of interposers, decap sheets and periphery TFT layers for memory packages.
why: Capital and time: tools already exist, cutting packaging capacity lead time from years to months.

title: Sacrificial printed fan-out exposes internal test nodes, then dissolves
idea: Worse: dedicate die area to hundreds of large probe pads and on-die test muxes. Flip: inkjet-print a temporary solvent-soluble polymer-and-silver fan-out over the wafer that connects tiny internal test points to large probe pads, test through it, then strip it before final passivation and bumping.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): probe-pad and test-mux area (~2-4% of die) shrinks, with deeper analog visibility into sense amps during test.

title: Electrohydrodynamic-jet printed nano-copper microbumps for memory stacking
idea: Worse: run lithography, seed, plating and etch steps to form every microbump. Flip: EHD-jet-print copper nanoparticle pillars at ~10 um pitch directly onto pads and sinter them in a maskless additive bumping step.
why: HBM cost and capital (fact 6): removes bump masks and plating lines, with denser I/O at lower capex.

title: Printed micro-heater film for fast wafer-level retention binning
idea: Worse: profile retention with slow chamber bakes so rows are never binned individually. Flip: laminate a printed resistive heater film at the probe-chuck interface that steps each die through precise temperatures in seconds while BIST logs per-row retention, storing bins for retention-aware refresh.
why: Refresh (fact 3): cheap per-row retention bins enable 2-4x longer refresh for most rows.

title: Origami chip-on-flex stack folds dies around a printed shared bus
idea: Worse: stack dies rigidly with TSVs and microbumps. Flip: mount thin dies at intervals along a roll-to-roll-printed flex tape carrying a shared command and data bus plus printed passives, then fold it accordion-style into a 3D stack bonded at one edge.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and capital: no TSVs and known-good-die assembly on roll-to-roll lines, giving cheaper capacity stacks.
